content.text: Describing his own search before he met his teacher, Vivekananda recalled: this man came to live near Calcutta, sending out sceptics by the hundreds every year, yet the great men from the different universities used to come and listen to him. 'I heard of this man, and I went to hear him. He looked just like an ordinary man, with nothing remarkable about him... and I thought, "Can this man be a great teacher?" I crept near to him and asked him the question which I had been asking others all my life: "Do you believe in God, Sir?"'
content.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

content.text: To his question the teacher, Sri Ramakrishna, answered simply, 'Yes.' 'Can you prove it, Sir?' 'Yes.' 'How?' 'Because I see Him just as I see you here, only in a much intenser sense.' Vivekananda recalled: 'That impressed me at once. For the first time I had found a man who dared to say that he saw God, that religion was a reality, to be felt, to be sensed...I began to come near that man, day after day, and I actually saw that religion could be given. One touch, one glance, can make a whole life change... when I myself saw this man, all scepticism was brushed aside.'
content.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

content.text: Of what he learned from his Master, Vivekananda taught: 'Religion is not talk, nor doctrines, nor theories, nor is it sectarianism. Religion cannot live in sects and societies. It is the relation between the soul and God... Religion does not consist in erecting temples, or building churches, or attending public worship. It is not to be found in books, nor in words, nor in lectures, nor in organizations. Religion consists in realization... The first ideal of this attempt to realize religion is that of renunciation.'
content.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

content.text: On the harmony of religions — the teaching that would carry him to the world stage at Chicago — Vivekananda said: 'The religions of the world are not contradictory nor antagonistic; they are but various phases of One Eternal Religion... we must respect all religions and we must try to accept them all as far as we can... "As different rivers, taking their start from different mountains, running crooked or straight, all come and mingle their waters in the ocean, so the different sects, with their different points of view, at last all come unto Thee."'
content.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

content.text: As Ramakrishna's fame drew ever larger crowds in his final illness, 'his intense love for mankind would not let him refuse to help even the humblest of the thousands who sought his aid,' though 'a vital throat disorder' had developed. Asked why he did not turn his own spiritual power to curing himself, he replied, 'My friend, I have thought you were a sage, but you talk like other men of the world. This mind has been given to the Lord, do you mean to say that I should take it back?' After his Master's death, Vivekananda and the other young disciples who carried on his work 'met with great antagonism, but they persevered' as wandering Sannyasins begging through the very streets where some had been born to first-class families.
content.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

content.text: In an address delivered to his countrymen during his return journey across India after the Parliament of Religions, Vivekananda called on them to reclaim their dignity: 'Oh India, forget not that your ideal woman is Sita, Savitri, Damayanti... forget not that from your very birth, you are sacrificed for the Mother... Hero, take courage, be proud that you are an Indian, — say, in pride, "I am an Indian, every Indian is my brother"... "the ignorant Indian, the poor Indian, the Brahman Indian, the Pariah Indian, is my brother."'
content.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

content.text: Vivekananda distilled his Master Sri Ramakrishna's message to the modern world in words that became the charter of his own life's work: 'Do not care for doctrines, do not care for dogmas, or sects, or churches or temples; they count for little compared with the essence of existence in each man which is spirituality... Earn that, first acquire that, and criticise no one, for all doctrines and creeds have some good in them... Be spiritual and realize truth for yourself.'
content.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'
